title: DIBench: Benchmarking Decision Integrity of GUI-based Mobile Agents Under Deceptive Injections

paper.title: DIBench: Benchmarking Decision Integrity of GUI-based Mobile Agents Under Deceptive Injections
paper.abstract:
Abstract As GUI-based mobile agents rapidly progress, rigorous safety evaluation of their autonomous decision-making in realistic app interfaces becomes increasingly critical.
Existing benchmarks mainly focus on execution-level anomalies using task success or hijack rates, but fail to capture the in-task goal deviation risk in multi-candidate selection tasks,
where the decision may be steered toward an attacker-specified target, even in violation of instruction-implied constraints (e.g., cheapest/highest-rated), without any overt execution anomalies.
We present DIBench , a decision integrity benchmark for measuring this risk in mobile agents.
DIBench covers 7 commercial and 3 simulated apps with 5 task types.
Under a threat model restricted to non-privileged UI content, we construct 8 deceptive injection probe instantiations that can steer critical selections without overt anomalies.
The benchmark includes 1,000 clean and 36,672 injected instances, with a unified protocol and integrity metrics for comparison.
Experiments spanning 4 agent frameworks and 7 base models show that completion-based evaluation can overestimate agent trustworthiness and miss decision-integrity risks: deceptive injections steer selections and shift early action policies, inflating completion rates and creating a misleading illusion of safety.
Common defenses, including detection, image preprocessing, and prompt reminders, yield inconsistent integrity gains.
Overall, DIBench provides a unified, reproducible benchmark to quantify the risk of in-task goal deviation in mobile agents and enable comparable evaluations of safety defenses.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have substantially improved cross-modal understanding and reasoning Bai et al. (2025a) ; OpenAI (2025) , enabling GUI mobile agents to autonomously perform multi-step interactions in real-world mobile apps Liu et al. (2025a) ; Rawles et al. (2024) ; Li et al. (2025) . Such agents are increasingly deployed in high-frequency scenarios—including shopping, food ordering, and travel planning—to filter options, verify details, and confirm choices Zhou et al. (2023) ; Lyu et al. (2025) . Because an agent’s output may directly trigger real transactions and shape security-sensitive decisions involving private or sensitive information, it is urgent to systematically characterize and validate the security and trustworthiness of mobile agent systems Chen et al. (2025b) ; Mathur et al. (2019) ; Lin et al. (2025) . Prior work has primarily evaluated mobile-agent security from the execution perspective Chen et al. (2025e) ; Chen et al. (2025c) ; Lee et al. (2026) ; Yang et al. (2025) ; Du et al. (2025) ; Liu et al. (2025b) , focusing on observable anomalies such as prompt-injection-induced task hijacking, unauthorized tool invocations, or interaction traces that visibly deviate from expected behavior. Accordingly, common metrics revolve around task completion rate and hijacking success rate Liu et al. (2025b) ; Liao et al. (2025) ; Lu et al. (2025) ; Evtimov et al. (2025) ; Chen et al. (2025a) , and many evaluations implicitly assume that flow-correct completion implies a trustworthy final choice Kara et al. (2025) ; Yehudai et al. (2025) . However, in real scenarios where multi-candidate selection is central, this assumption does not always hold Kang et al. (2025) ; Gebreegziabher et al. (2026) ; Xue et al. (2023) . In multi-candidate selection tasks on mobile devices, an agent may complete the workflow without privilege escalation, hijacking, or anomalous trajectories, yet still make a manipulated final selection Yang et al. (2024) ; Gebreegziabher et al. (2026) ; Kim et al. (2024) . We define this as In-Task Goal Deviation : under deceptive injection, the agent completes the task but its final choice is redirected toward an attacker-specified option, potentially even violating instruction-implied constraints (e.g., lowest price or highest rating) outside the acceptable set, thereby compromising decision integrity . Crucially, attackers need not alter the instruction or control flow: platform-permitted UI content (e.g., titles or images) can steer critical choices without overt anomalies, while completion-based signals are often insensitive—causing such deviations to be missed by evaluations focused on completion or trajectory anomalies. Although recent anecdotal evidence suggests that mobile agents can be steered by on-screen content during selection Yang et al. (2024) ; Wu et al. (2024) , the community still lacks a reproducible framework for measuring such decision-layer risks under controlled and comparable conditions. Key gaps remain: (1) no explicit security model for targeted in-task goal deviation; (2) the lack of a scalable benchmark suite of multi-candidate selection tasks spanning both commercial and simulated apps; and (3) no unified protocol or decision-integrity metrics for comparing agent frameworks, base models, and defenses. Our benchmark. To address this gap, we introduce DIBench , a benchmark for evaluating the decision integrity of mobile GUI agents in multi-candidate selection tasks. DIBench focuses on key decision states where the agent must compare candidates and select one according to instruction-implied constraints. For each task, we define an instruction I I , a candidate set C C , and an acceptable set A ⁡ ( I , C ) A(I,C) of semantically valid choices. We then construct paired benign and injected instances under matched task conditions, changing only UI-visible content at the critical decision point. This design allows DIBench to measure whether injected content causes targeted steering or decision degradation while controlling for the original task, candidate set, and non-visual context. DIBench covers both real-world and controlled environments. It includes 7 commercial mobile apps and 3 simulated apps across 5 categories of multi-candidate selection tasks, including exploratory, exact-match, cost-based, spatio-temporal, and quality/popularity-based decisions. To evaluate deceptive decision influence, we design 8 injection probe instantiations spanning textual overlays, image-embedded content, and visual perturbations. Overall, DIBench contains 1,000 benign instances and 36,672 injected instances, together with structured annotations for candidates, injection anchors, acceptable sets, target candidates, and paired evaluation. The benchmark further provides a unified configuration suite and standardized defense hooks, enabling comparable evaluation across agent frameworks, base models, and mitigation strategies under the same task and threat settings. Our findings. Using DIBench, we conduct evaluations spanning 4 mobile-agent frameworks and 7 base models across real commercial and simulated app settings. We make the following observations: (1) completion-oriented metrics can overestimate agent trustworthiness by missing decision-integrity risks, as deceptive injections can increase task completion while achieving high targeted steering rates (e.g., TCR rises from 42.0% to 72.4% with 45.8% ASR in commercial apps), creating a misleading illusion of improved safety under completion-based evaluation; (2) injections alter the decision process, reducing exploration and verification while inducing earlier commitment to injected targets; (3) common defenses remain unreliable, with detection recall dropping sharply on low-saliency injections and preprocessing sometimes increasing ASR; and (4) decision deviation is context-dependent, emerging from interactions among attack semantics, model behavior, framework constraints, UI structure, and task characteristics. Overall, DIBench provides a systematic testbed for evaluating decision-layer robustness of mobile GUI agents beyond execution-level safety metrics.

sections.heading: Mobile GUI Agents and Multi-Candidate Decision Making.
sections.text: Mobile GUI agents typically operate in a closed observe–plan–act loop Tang et al. (2025a) ; Zhou et al. (2025) ; Gou et al. (2025) . Observations are derived from screenshots and accessibility trees, from which agents perform UI grounding and execute low-level actions such as tapping, scrolling, typing, and navigation Rawles et al. (2024) ; Hu et al. (2025) . Compared to scripted automation, MLLM-based agents can extract semantic cues from multimodal interfaces and conduct high-level planning across apps and pages, enabling complex workflows in real mobile environments Liu et al. (2025a) . In many real-world applications such as e-commerce and food delivery, task structure is inherently centered on comparison and selection over a candidate set Allouah et al. (2025) ; Wang et al. (2026) . Search results, filtered lists, and recommendation panels naturally form candidate sets, and agents must balance exploration (e.g., paging and filtering) with committing to a final choice. While existing evaluations often emphasize whether an agent completes the interaction flow, whether the within-set selection aligns with instruction semantics is a distinct and critical dimension of agent behavior. sections.heading: Security and Evaluation of LLM-driven Mobile Agents.
sections.text: Existing security evaluations of mobile GUI agents fall into three directions. (i) Trustworthiness under high-stakes tasks evaluates safety in privacy-, finance-, or social-related settings, e.g., MLA-Trust Yang et al. (2025) , MSB Lee et al. (2026) , and GhostEI Chen et al. (2025c) . (ii) Robustness to system-level interruptions measures recovery under runtime perturbations such as permission dialogs, notifications, or state changes, as in D-GARA Chen et al. (2025d) . (iii) Security against third-party content injection restricts adversaries to non-privileged parties who influence agents through legitimate UI content and evaluates risks from indirect prompt injection or UI deception, e.g., NAE Du et al. (2025) , AgentHazard Liu et al. (2025b) , SecMoba Yang et al. (2024) , and the injection setting in GhostEI Chen et al. (2025c) . Complementarily, AgentScan studies end-to-end exploitability across the LLM/GUI/System stack Wu et al. (2025) . Table 1 summarizes this distinction across representative mobile-agent security benchmarks. Despite these differences, existing evaluations mainly focus on execution-level observables, such as task completion, interruption, hijacking, or unauthorized actions, rather than whether the final choice within a candidate set remains aligned with instruction semantics.

sections.heading: Decision-Layer Risks in Multi-Candidate Selection.
sections.text: A mobile agent can complete a task without any observable anomalies yet still make an attacker-steered choice at the selection stage Yang et al. (2024) ; Wu et al. (2024) ; Zhang et al. (2025) . In such cases, the agent performs browsing, filtering, and submission as expected, but ultimately selects a candidate promoted by deceptive UI content, potentially even violating the user’s objective. Because such risks involve no hijacking or execution anomalies, they are typically missed by existing execution-focused evaluations. However, these behaviors are often framed as isolated cases or capability gaps rather than as a systematic security risk Yang et al. (2024) . Consequently, decision-layer risks induced purely through platform-permitted UI content remain insufficiently formalized, and a reproducible, comparable evaluation framework is still missing. sections.heading: 3 DIBench Construction
sections.text: DIBench is designed to evaluate in-task goal deviation in multi-candidate selection tasks, where a mobile agent completes the workflow but its final choice is steered toward an attacker-specified target. To isolate this decision-layer risk, DIBench adopts a non-privileged UI-content threat model : the adversary can influence the agent only through platform-permitted on-screen content (e.g., titles or images), without modifying instructions, prompts, or control flow. Figure 1 illustrates DIBench.

sections.heading: 3.1 Benchmark Components
sections.text: DIBench consists of three core components: environments, a task suite, and injection probes. Overall, it includes 7 commercial apps and 3 simulated apps across 5 task categories, with 1,000 benign instances and 36,672 injected instances, as summarized in Table 2 .

sections.heading: 3.1.1 Environments
sections.text: To balance real-world validity and controllability, DIBench includes both real-world commercial applications and controlled simulated environments. Real-world commercial apps. We select 7 popular mobile apps—AliExpress, Amazon, Booking, Fantuan, Foodpanda, Tripadvisor, and Walmart—covering search, booking, and shopping scenarios. These apps provide realistic UI complexity and diversity. Due to ethical constraints, we do not upload adversarial images or injected merchant content to commercial platforms. Instead, we extract fixed decision states from real apps and apply controlled screenshot-level injections, keeping benign and injected inputs comparable while avoiding impacts on real users, merchants, or live services. Controlled simulated apps. For dynamic execution and mechanism analysis, we implement 3 controlled simulated apps: a Meituan-style food-ordering app, an online-shopping app, and a travel-itinerary planning app. These environments preserve multi-level browsing and multi-candidate selection patterns while reducing task-irrelevant UI noise, yielding deterministic and reproducible multi-step interactions with fixed candidate sets, hierarchy, and ordering. Crucially, they also support an end-to-end “ content publication/update → \rightarrow frontend rendering ” path, allowing injected content to be treated as a controlled variable for process-level analysis.

sections.heading: 3.1.2 Task Suite
sections.text: Tasks are constructed for each app using unified templates, where the user objective and candidate set are explicitly specified to ensure a well-defined correct choice under benign conditions. Each task defines an instruction I I , a candidate set C = { c 1 , … , c n } C=\{c_{1},\ldots,c_{n}\} , and an acceptable set A ⁡ ( I , C ) A(I,C) of semantically valid choices. We consider five categories: Exploratory , Exact Match , Cost , Spatio-Temporal , and Quality/Popularity . Exploratory tasks admit all candidates ( A ⁡ ( I , C ) = C A(I,C)=C ), whereas the other categories impose UI-observable constraints or preferences and yield 1 ≤ | A ⁡ ( I , C ) | < | C | 1\leq|A(I,C)|<|C| . Exact Match filters candidates via discrete predicates (e.g., brand, name, destination); Cost minimizes price-related attributes (e.g., price, delivery fee); Spatio-Temporal minimizes distance, delivery time, or itinerary duration; and Quality/Popularity maximizes signals such as rating, sales volume, or review count. This taxonomy supports stratified analysis of how task semantics and constraint structures affect susceptibility to targeted steering, while acceptability annotations provide instruction-level correctness labels. sections.heading: 3.1.3 Injection Probes and Injected Instances
sections.text: DIBench introduces standardized, parameterized probes that modify UI-visible content at critical decision states while preserving instructions, candidate sets, and interaction flow. Probe taxonomy. We consider three carriers: text-overlay probes applied to candidate titles or key regions (Title) Mo et al. (2025) ; Faghih et al. (2025) ; Tang et al. (2025b) ; Shi et al. (2025) , image-embedded text probes (Cover) Yang et al. (2024) ; Gong et al. (2025) ; Shayegani et al. (2023) , and visual perturbations without explicit text (Pert.) Wang et al. (2025a) ; Jiang et al. (2025) ; Zhao et al. (2025) ; Aichberger et al. (2025) . Probe instantiations. We implement 8 probe variants: five text-based variants (Naive, Escape, Context Ignore, Fake Completion, and Combined) applied to Title regions Liu et al. (2024) ; Jia et al. (2025) , and three cross-channel variants derived from the Combined semantics— Combined-C (Cover only), Combined-TC (Title and Cover), and Combined-P (Perturbation)—for controlled comparison of carrier effects. Illustrative examples are shown in Figure 3 in Appendix. Injected instances and pairing. Each injected instance is defined as a tuple of decision state, target candidate, and probe instantiation. Only UI-visible content is modified, while instructions, candidate sets, and interaction flow remain unchanged. Each injected instance is paired with a benign counterpart under identical task conditions, enabling controlled comparison.

sections.heading: 3.2 Instance Generation Pipeline
sections.text: DIBench instances are constructed through a multi-stage pipeline that produces benign instances, injected variants, and acceptable-set annotations. Step 1: Benign instance construction and decision point localization. For each task, we execute a benign reference trajectory and identify the key decision point. We extract its evaluation input as a benign instance consisting of: (i) a screenshot of the critical selection interface and (ii) fixed non-visual context prior to selection (e.g., query history, filters, or sorting). The non-visual context is held constant across comparisons, yielding a reproducible decision state ⟨ screenshot , fixed context ⟩ \langle\textit{screenshot},\textit{fixed context}\rangle . Step 2: Structured candidate parsing and injection anchors. At each decision state, an MLLM-assisted annotation interface initializes candidate parsing C = { c 1 , … , c n } C=\{c_{1},\ldots,c_{n}\} by detecting candidate boundaries and extracting UI-visible text and attributes. These outputs serve only as preliminary drafts; human annotators verify, correct, and finalize all candidate sets, attributes, and anchors. Each candidate is assigned a stable ID, with injection anchors such as Title and Cover extracted. We release reusable annotations including (i) general annotations with candidate IDs and anchor identifiers for screenshot-level and backend injections, and (ii) screenshot-level annotations with pixel anchors and style parameters for controlled perturbations with minimal layout distortion. Step 3: Injection instance generation under a unified specification. Given benign instances and candidate anchors, injected instances are generated under a unified specification: decision state + target candidate + probe instantiation \textit{decision state}+\textit{target candidate}+\textit{probe instantiation} . For real commercial apps (screenshot-level injection), injected screenshots are produced via image-level overlay or embedding without modifying the underlying UI structure, reusing pixel anchors and style parameters from Step 2 to minimize non-semantic perturbations. For controlled simulated apps (backend injection), injections are applied to candidate fields (e.g., Title or Cover) along the content publication pipeline and rendered by the frontend during evaluation. Fixed candidate sets and UI structures ensure that injection semantics remain the primary controlled variable and enable process-level analysis. Step 4: Acceptable-set A ⁡ ( I , C ) A(I,C) annotation. We construct A ⁡ ( I , C ) A(I,C) using structured candidate attributes from Step 2. For exploratory tasks, A ⁡ ( I , C ) = C A(I,C)=C ; for deterministic tasks (e.g., “cheapest”, “fastest”, “highest-rated”), GPT-5.2 is used as an initial label proposer to identify candidates satisfying the instruction-induced criterion. All proposed labels are independently verified by two human annotators, with disagreements adjudicated by a third; final labels are human-determined, and ambiguous or unverifiable instances are removed. The labeling pipeline is separated from all evaluated GPT-5.2 agent configurations to avoid label–model coupling. Step 5: Instance normalization and release. Each task is normalized into a unified benchmark entry containing: (i) task specification (instruction, environment conditions, task type); (ii) decision state (screenshot and fixed context); (iii) candidate annotations and anchors (candidate IDs, anchor identifiers, and pixel/style parameters); (iv) injection specification (paired injected screenshots or backend injection definitions); and (v) labels and indices ( A ⁡ ( I , C ) A(I,C) , benign/injected pairing, target candidate, and probe instantiation). Entries also include standardized metadata (e.g., task ID, app/task type, candidate indices, probe type) to support cross-framework evaluation and stratified analysis.

sections.heading: 3.3.1 Evaluation Protocol
sections.text: Paired evaluation. For each task, we construct a benign decision state and its injected variants (see § 3.2 ). During evaluation, the agent receives the same instruction and identical non-visual context ; the only difference is whether the critical selection screenshot contains injected content. Each task is evaluated R R times (default R = 10 R{=}10 ) with matched seeds for paired benign/injected runs, and metrics are computed as empirical averages. Outcome definition. We define the outcome as the agent’s final selection , mapped to C ~ = C ∪ { ⊥ } \tilde{C}=C\cup\{\bot\} , where ⊥ \bot denotes no committed choice. Outcomes are labeled as Correct ( c ^ ∈ A ⁡ ( I , C ) \hat{c}\in A(I,C) ), Incorrect ( c ^ ∈ C ∖ A ⁡ ( I , C ) \hat{c}\in C\setminus A(I,C) ), or Failure ( c ^ = ⊥ \hat{c}=\bot ). An out-of-band monitor records the selected candidate ID without affecting agent behavior. Under deceptive inputs, paired benign and injected conditions allow us to distinguish targeted manipulation , which steers the agent to a specific target candidate, from untargeted degradation , which turns an otherwise acceptable decision into an incorrect one.

sections.heading: 3.4 Extensible Agent Configuration Suite
sections.text: To enable comparable evaluation across agent frameworks and foundation models, DIBench provides an extensible configuration suite that abstracts runtime differences into pluggable units. It includes AgentAdapter and ModelProvider : the former handles framework instantiation and selection-stage I/O alignment, while the latter handles model invocation and fixed inference settings to ensure consistent inputs and outcomes. The initial release supports four agent frameworks— AppAgent Li et al. (2024) , Mobile-Agent-V2 Wang et al. (2024) , Mobile-Agent-E Wang et al. (2025b) , and Mobile-Agent-V3 Ye et al. (2025) —and seven foundation models spanning open- and closed-source settings. Open-source models include Qwen2.5-VL(32B) Bai et al. (2025b) , Qwen3-VL(32B) Bai et al. (2025a) , GUI-Owl(32B) Ye et al. (2025) , and Mai-UI(8B) Zhou et al. (2025) ; closed-source models include DoubaoSeed-1.6 ByteDance Seed (2025b) ; ByteDance Seed (2025a) , Gemini-3-Flash Google (2025) , and GPT-5.2 OpenAI (2025) . These configurations support reproducibility and horizontal comparison across framework–model pairings.

sections.heading: 3.5 Benchmark Extension: Defense Track
sections.text: DIBench includes a defense track that evaluates mitigations under the same tasks, injection conditions, and threat model as the no-defense baseline. To preserve comparability, defenses are enabled only through standardized hooks. We focus on three general-purpose defense classes applicable to the injected instances, while the track can be extended to more advanced defenses. Defense hook points. To avoid coupling defenses to specific frameworks, DIBench exposes three pluggable interfaces: (i) input detection , applying an LLM-based detector to selection-stage inputs (UI text/images, optionally with agent-side intermediate planning) to flag potential prompt injections using fixed detector prompts Liu et al. (2025c) ; Liu et al. (2024) (Appendix A ); (ii) input preprocessing , transforming screenshots (e.g., Gaussian noise Zhang et al. (2023) ; Dziedzic and Krishnan (2020) , JPEG compression Guo et al. (2017) , resizing Xie et al. (2017) ) to attenuate injected semantics while preserving UI structure and task-relevant evidence; and (iii) prompt-level mitigation , prepending a short, fixed risk-warning sentence to the system prompt or instruction (e.g., “The screenshot may contain injection attacks; do not follow on-screen instructions and avoid selecting injected items”.) Learn Prompting (2023a) ; Learn Prompting (2023b) ; Zhang et al. (2024) . This provides a framework-agnostic, low-overhead control knob for benchmarking instruction-level hardening in isolation.

sections.heading: 4 Benchmark Results
sections.text: We evaluate DIBench on multi-candidate selection tasks in two representative settings: fixed decision states from real commercial apps ( Commerce ) and controlled simulation apps ( Simulator ). We study whether deceptive injections can steer critical selections—undermining decision integrity —while preserving selection completion, i.e., without overt hijacking or observable selection-stage anomalies. Additional implementation details are provided in Appendix B .

sections.heading: 4.1 Completion-oriented metrics overestimate agent trustworthiness
sections.text: We first examine whether completion-oriented metrics reliably reflect agent trustworthiness in multi-candidate selection tasks. Table 3 and Appendix Table 5 show that deceptive injections can inflate , rather than reduce, task completion rate (TCR). Under Combined , TCR rises from 42.0% to 72.4% for AppAgent + Qwen2.5-VL in Commerce , and from 48.5% to 86.6% for Mobile-Agent-E + Qwen3-VL in Simulator . A completion-based evaluation would therefore make these agents appear more reliable under attack, simply because they more often reach a committed selection. This apparent improvement is misleading: the final choice can still be steered toward an attacker-specified target. COR can also increase in some settings, e.g., from 28.4% to 46.9% for AppAgent + Qwen2.5-VL in Commerce and from 41.2% to 64.6% for Mobile-Agent-V3 + Qwen2.5-VL in Simulator , showing that instruction-level acceptability alone does not rule out target steering. ASR exposes this hidden steering mode. Despite higher TCR/COR, ASR reaches 45.8% for AppAgent + Qwen2.5-VL in Commerce and 49.8% for Mobile-Agent-V3 + Qwen3-VL in Simulator . Thus, completion-oriented evaluation can overestimate trustworthiness: deceptive UI content may make agents appear more successful while silently increasing attacker control over the final decision. This trend persists across additional base models (Appendix Table 8 ). Takeaway. Completion-based evaluation can overestimate the trustworthiness of mobile agents in multi-candidate selection tasks. Deceptive injections may increase TCR, and sometimes even COR, while steering the final choice toward an attacker-specified target. ASR reveals this hidden decision-integrity risk by measuring attacker control over the committed selection rather than whether the selection merely appears completed. sections.heading: 4.2 Deceptive injections shift decision trajectories
sections.text: We now examine how deceptive injection changes the agent’s action trajectory before the final decision. Figure 2 shows that across four frameworks and two model families, under Combined Attack , the proportion of selection actions consistently increases while delayed-decision actions (e.g., Filter/Search/Swipe/Answer) decrease. This shift suggests that agents spend less time in exploration and verification stages and more frequently transition to selection actions. This behavioral change also helps explain why TCR sometimes increases under attack in Section 4.1 , as agents reach a terminal action more quickly, regardless of whether the final choice is correct. In addition, as shown in Figure 4 in Appendix, the black curves (No Attack) exhibit stable baseline selection patterns across the Others and candidate indices. Under attack (colored curves), the overall distribution shape largely persists: aside from the designated target index, the relative ordering among other indices remains similar. The main difference is a pronounced peak at the target dimension accompanied by a consistent decline in Others (refusal and continued exploration). This pattern suggests that the attack converts actions that would otherwise lead to no submission or continued browsing into submissions at the target option. Takeaway. Deceptive injection affects not only which option is selected but also how decisions are made: it compresses pre-decision deliberation by reducing exploration and verification actions and inducing earlier commitment. This preserves superficially plausible trajectories and stable distributional structure while enabling targeted steering, making such attacks stealthy and difficult to detect with completion-oriented metrics alone. sections.heading: 4.3 Current general defenses remain unreliable
sections.text: Using the defense track of DIBench, we evaluate three defense classes— detection-based , image-processing-based , and prompt-based —under in-task goal deviation. Complete defense results are provided in Appendix. Detection-based defenses. Table 4 shows that detection achieves near-saturated recall on strong semantic-overwrite attacks (e.g., Context Ignore and Combined ). However, this advantage does not extend to more naturalistic injections: recall drops sharply to 18.2% and 21.2% for Naive and Escape , respectively, suggesting under-detection of low-saliency overlays. Moreover, adding planning signals does not consistently improve performance and can reduce recall below single-modality settings with substantial cross-framework variation. This pattern is consistent with the difficulty of extracting verifiable injection evidence from heterogeneous inputs, where additional modalities may introduce noise or conflicting signals. Image-processing-based defenses. Table 6 shows that preprocessing operations (e.g., noise, compression, and resizing) have inconsistent effects on ASR: the same method may reduce targeted steering in some cases but increase it in others. For example, noise injection can raise ASR from 45.8% to 60.0% in one setting while reducing it from 52.2% to 41.3% in another, with similar trends observed for compression and resizing. The root cause is that preprocessing is not semantic-aware: it can simultaneously weaken benign decision evidence and distort steering cues, sometimes reducing attribute verifiability and pushing agents toward locally salient signals that amplify selection shift. Prompt-based defenses. Table 7 shows that prompt-based defenses can substantially reduce ASR—often by over 30% for strong attacks—while sometimes improving COR. However, these gains are not consistent: in some configurations, prompts are ineffective or even increase ASR, and can incur noticeable COR drops. This suggests that prompt defenses act as soft constraints whose reliability depends on prompt orchestration and model compliance; reproducible decision-integrity gains likely require integrating key-attribute verification and UI-evidence referencing into the agent pipeline to reduce prompt sensitivity and avoid COR degradation. Takeaway. Existing defenses do not provide stable, generalizable improvements in decision integrity. Detection is sensitive to saliency and struggles with low-signal injections, preprocessing lacks semantic awareness and can distort decision evidence, and prompt-based defenses rely on fragile behavioral alignment. More fundamentally, these limitations stem from a mismatch: in-task goal deviation arises from failures in grounded evidence use and verification, whereas current general defenses do not enforce consistent, evidence-grounded decision-making.

sections.heading: 4.4 Additional analysis
sections.text: We further examine factors that modulate the extent of in-task goal deviation; detailed results are provided in Appendix C . Deviation strength is not governed by a single factor, but by the joint effect of attack semantics, agent-framework constraints, base-model characteristics, injection-carrier visibility, app interface structure, and task type. Strong semantic-coverage probes raise the potential upper bound of target-specific steering, while the realized ASR is amplified or suppressed by the model–framework combination and by what the interface and task structure permit. These results suggest that in-task goal deviation is inherently context-dependent, and that robustness cannot be reliably inferred from a single attack setting or platform. Evaluating such risks therefore requires considering diverse decision contexts and the interactions among contributing factors.

sections.heading: 5 Discussion and Future Work
sections.text: Decision integrity risks in mobile agents. Multimodal LLM-based mobile GUI agents can complete multi-step tasks in real applications, yet safety evaluation remains largely execution-centric (e.g., completion, absence of failures). Our results show that execution correctness and decision trustworthiness can be decoupled: agents may complete tasks without observable anomalies while being steered away from intended choices, resulting in in-task goal deviation . This risk arises from platform-permitted UI content (e.g., titles or images) that implicitly influences decisions without altering instructions or execution flow. Consequently, completion- and correctness-based metrics can underestimate decision-level risks and may even suggest improved performance under attack. This is critical in deployment, where users observe task completion but cannot detect subtle decision manipulation. Decision integrity should therefore be treated as a distinct layer in agent safety evaluation. Evaluating decision integrity. DIBench addresses this gap via paired (benign/injected) protocols and decision-integrity metrics, enabling cross-model comparison. TCR and COR fail to reflect manipulation and may create a false sense of safety, whereas ASR directly captures target steering. Trajectory analysis further shows that attacks weaken exploration and verification, inducing earlier commitment while preserving plausible interaction patterns. These findings highlight the need to evaluate evidence use and verification, beyond outcome-level metrics. Limitations and future work. DIBench is a reproducible academic benchmark for isolating decision-layer risks via controlled benign/injected comparisons. Our evaluation covers open research mobile-agent frameworks but not commercial or OEM-deployed assistants, such as AI phones or pre-installed voice assistants, limiting external validity. Still, DIBench captures a core risk: UI-visible content can influence model-driven selection without modifying user instructions or control flow. Future work should extend DIBench to production systems and long-horizon multi-decision tasks. Existing defenses are limited to general-purpose hooks, including detection, preprocessing, and prompt reminders; stronger evidence-grounded defenses, such as structured attribute comparison and pre-commit verification, remain important directions. Ethics statement. DIBench evaluates decision-level safety risks in mobile GUI agents under realistic UI conditions. A fully realistic setup would require publishing injected content to commercial platforms or interacting with live services, which could affect users, merchants, or platform operators without consent. We therefore avoid state-changing actions on external services: commercial-app evaluations use fixed decision states and screenshot-level injections only, without publishing content, modifying third-party platforms, executing transactions, or collecting private user data. Simulated apps are used for controlled mechanism analysis. DIBench is released for measurement and defense research, not for one-click attack deployment against external apps, with dataset documentation.

We synthesize evidence from Tables 3 , 5 , 8 , and 9 , together with Figures 5 ,and 6 (injection carriers, cross-application, task types, and decision dynamics), and analyze each factor in detail. (1) Attack paradigm: stronger semantic coverage yields a higher ASR upper bound and better cross-environment stability. Attacks with “context overriding / instruction rewriting” semantics (i.e., Context Ignore and Combined ) achieve higher and more stable ASR than Naive and Escape . In Commerce (Table 3 ), Mobile-Agent-V3 + Qwen3-VL increases from 11.0%/12.9% under Naive/Escape to 44.6% under Context Ignore and 52.2% under Combined ; in Simulator (Table 5 ), it rises from 18.7%/19.3% to 43.3%/49.8%. Once an injection can override task context and provide an executable substitute instruction, it shifts probability mass toward the target candidate, raising ASR and improving cross-environment consistency. (2) Framework modulation: the same attack exhibits different tractability across frameworks, with model–framework interactions. Attack strength depends not only on the attack but also on framework-imposed constraints and action policies, and relative vulnerability varies with the base model. Under Qwen3-VL, Mobile-Agent-V3 and Mobile-Agent-E show high ASR under strong attacks in both environments: in Commerce (Table 3 ), Combined reaches 52.2%/50.3%, and in Simulator (Table 5 ), 49.8%/48.4%; in contrast, Mobile-Agent-V2 is lower (24.3%/27.9% for Context Ignore/Combined in Simulator ). Under Qwen2.5-VL, however, AppAgent attains 44.5% ASR under Combined in Simulator , surpassing Mobile-Agent-V3 (30.7%) and Mobile-Agent-V2 (25.6%). This suggests that “framework vulnerability” is not monotonic in the framework alone but emerges from interactions between framework decision constraints and base-model alignment characteristics. With frameworks and environments fixed, strong semantic-coverage attacks show a stable ASR hierarchy: general-purpose open-source models attain the highest ASR, specialized open-source models are lower, and closed-source models are generally lowest. With Mobile-Agent-V3 in Simulator (Table 8 ), Qwen3-VL achieves 43.3%/49.8% under Context Ignore/Combined , while Qwen2.5-VL reaches 31.8%/30.7%; GUI-Owl drops to 19.9%/19.3%, and closed-source models decrease further (e.g., DoubaoSeed-1.6 5.4%/7.5%, Gemini-3-Flash 5.0%/8.7%, GPT-5.2 5.9%/3.8%). Overall, general open-source models are more susceptible to instruction-style semantic overriding, while specialized open-source and closed-source models are more resistant, plausibly because general models emphasize broad instruction following and UI-semantic compliance, whereas specialized models rely more on structured grounding and closed-source models may incorporate stronger defenses and more conservative policies. (4) Injection carriers: gains are dominated by “readability × \times semantic weight”, with Title most effective but subject to saturation. Stable target steering occurs only when injections appear in high-weight semantic regions that the model can directly read; among carriers, Title coverage is typically most effective, while additional coverage may saturate or even degrade performance. In Table 9 , across frameworks and both base models, Title/Cover coverage usually yields ASR in the 20%–50% range and accounts for nearly all peak values, whereas Pert. is consistently lower (about 6%–16%) and never attains the maximum (“Summary # Max” = 0). Title+Cover also does not guarantee stronger attacks: under Qwen3-VL+Combined , the ASR of Mobile-Agent-E drops from 48.8% (Title) to 33.0%, Mobile-Agent-V3 from 49.9% to 40.6%, and AppAgent from 37.0% to 30.1%. This suggests Title carries high semantic weight, but multi-region coverage may be redundant and saturate attention; it may also reflect resolution/legibility effects or model–pipeline differences across regions. By contrast, Pert. behaves as weak noise: under the current implementation, UI rendering often disrupts target alignment, preventing perturbations from reliably encoding executable instructions and resulting in consistently low attack success; nevertheless, such rendering-layer anomalies can still cause agent decisions to deviate substantially from normal behavior. Across apps, the relative ranking of attack paradigms largely persists (higher semantic-coverage attacks remain stronger), but the absolute ASR of the same strong attack depends heavily on how an app organizes interface information and decision pathways. In Figure 5 , Context Ignore and Combined consistently expand outward across most app/framework/model combinations, significantly exceeding Naive and Escape . Yet even under fixed strong attacks and configurations, ASR varies widely across apps, from low levels to near saturation. Peak heights also differ: Foodpanda yields consistently high ASR peaks; Walmart/Amazon show pronounced peaks under some framework–model pairings; whereas Booking/Tripadvisor remain low in most cases with limited gains. This suggests that app interface structure determines the “attackable space” for adversarial steering. Frameworks and models mainly amplify or suppress these pre-existing vulnerabilities; while peak heights and secondary peak locations may shift, the overall pattern of which apps are more sensitive or robust is rarely overturned. (6) Task types: constraint strength determines “whether steering is possible”, while verifiability determines “whether steering leads to wrong selections”. Strong attacks exhibit a consistent stratification across task types: tighter constraints make tasks harder to steer, whereas tasks that rely on continuous attribute ranking with high UI verification cost are more vulnerable to “completion with targeted mis-selection”. Figure 6 shows that under attack, Open-ended tasks shift substantial probability mass to Correct(Target) , reflecting preference rewriting without necessarily increasing errors, and Exact Match tasks maintain high Correct rates under both no-attack and attack conditions with limited growth in Wrong(Target) . In contrast, Cost and Quality/Pop tasks show a pronounced increase in Wrong(Target) under Combined Attack, becoming the dominant error source, while Spatio-Temporal tasks exhibit mixed behavior with increases in both Wrong(Target) and Wrong(Non-Target) . Overall, discrete entity predicates impose strong constraints that limit steering outside A ⁡ ( I , C ) A(I,C) , whereas continuous ranking tasks become susceptible once injections reduce attribute comparison and verification while preserving task completion. Figure 6: Selection distribution by task type on Simulator under No Attack (N.) vs. Combined Attack (A.) across agent frameworks and model families, showing shifts among Correct(Target), Wrong(Target), and Wrong(Non-Target) (stacked). Takeaway. In-task goal deviation strength emerges from a multiplicative coupling of factors: strong semantic-coverage attacks raise the ASR upper bound, but stable steering depends on framework decision constraints, base-model alignment/defenses, whether injections enter high-weight readable regions (e.g., Title), and the structural limits imposed by the app interface and task. Thus, attacks are not uniformly strong across settings; they are jointly amplified or suppressed by the model–framework combination within what the decision pathway permits. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed. • While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example (a) If the contribution is primarily a new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm. (b) If the contribution is primarily a new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully. (c) If the contribution is a new model (e.g., a large language model), then there should either be a way to access this model for reproducing the results or a way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset). (d) We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results. 5. Open access to data and code Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental material? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The abstract provides an anonymized code repository, and Section 3.2 states that normalized benchmark entries, annotations, injection specifications, labels, and metadata are packaged for release. The release is intended to support cross-framework reproduction and stratified analysis. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that paper does not include experiments requiring code. • Please see the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines ( https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy ) for more details. • While we encourage the release of code and data, we understand that this might not be possible, so [No] is an acceptable answer. Papers cannot be rejected simply for not including code, unless this is central to the contribution (e.g., for a new open-source benchmark). • The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to reproduce the results. See the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines ( https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy ) for more details. • The authors should provide instructions on data access and preparation, including how to access the raw data, preprocessed data, intermediate data, and generated data, etc. • The authors should provide scripts to reproduce all experimental results for the new proposed method and baselines. If only a subset of experiments are reproducible, they should state which ones are omitted from the script and why. • At submission time, to preserve anonymity, the authors should release anonymized versions (if applicable). • Providing as much information as possible in supplemental material (appended to the paper) is recommended, but including URLs to data and code is permitted. 6. Experimental setting/details Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The paper specifies the task suite, environments, injected-instance generation, paired benign/injected protocol, repeated evaluation with matched seeds, metrics, agent frameworks, base models, and defense settings in Sections 3 and 4. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • The experimental setting should be presented in the core of the paper to a level of detail that is necessary to appreciate the results and make sense of them. • The full details can be provided either with the code, in appendix, or as supplemental material. 7. Experiment statistical significance Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments? Answer: [No] Justification: The paper reports empirical averages from a large-scale paired benchmark evaluation. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper. • The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions). • The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to a library function, bootstrap, etc.) • The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors). • It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean. • It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report a 2-sigma error bar than state that they have a 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified. • For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates). • If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text. 8. Experiments compute resources Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the computer resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce the experiments? Answer: [No] Justification: Appendix B reports the local compute infrastructure used in our experiments. We do not report per-experiment runtime or total compute cost because the evaluation pipeline combines local execution, Android emulation, mobile UI interaction, and hosted closed-source model APIs; consequently, wall-clock time depends on factors such as API latency, provider-side scheduling, and UI interaction overhead that are not directly observable or consistently controlled by the authors. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • The paper should indicate the type of compute workers CPU or GPU, internal cluster, or cloud provider, including relevant memory and storage. • The paper should provide the amount of compute required for each of the individual experimental runs as well as estimate the total compute. • The paper should disclose whether the full research project required more compute than the experiments reported in the paper (e.g., preliminary or failed experiments that didn’t make it into the paper). 9. Code of ethics Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines ? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The paper includes an ethics statement explaining that real-app evaluations use fixed decision states and screenshot-level injections only, without publishing injected content, modifying third-party platforms, executing transactions, or collecting private user data. The benchmark is released for measurement and defense research rather than one-click attack deployment. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the authors have not reviewed the NeurIPS Code of Ethics. • If the authors answer [No] , they should explain the special circumstances that require a deviation from the Code of Ethics. • The authors should make sure to preserve anonymity (e.g., if there is a special consideration due to laws or regulations in their jurisdiction). 10. Broader impacts Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Sections 1, 5, and the ethics statement discuss the positive impact of improving decision-integrity evaluation for mobile GUI agents, as well as negative or dual-use risks from deceptive UI injections and potential misuse. The paper also explains safeguards used to avoid harm to users, merchants, and platforms during evaluation. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that there is no societal impact of the work performed. • If the authors answer [N/A] or [No] , they should explain why their work has no societal impact or why the paper does not address societal impact. • Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations. • The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied to particular applications, let alone deployments. However, if there is a direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that a generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster. • The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology. • If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how a system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML). 11. Safeguards Question: Does the paper describe safeguards that have been put in place for responsible release of data or models that have a high risk for misuse (e.g., pre-trained language models, image generators, or scraped datasets)? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The paper describes safeguards for the dual-use benchmark: commercial-app injections are performed only at the screenshot level, no content is published to live platforms, no transactions are executed, no private user data is collected, and the release is positioned for measurement and defense research with dataset documentation. Licenses for existing assets Question: Are the creators or original owners of assets (e.g., code, data, models), used in the paper, properly credited and are the license and terms of use explicitly mentioned and properly respected? Answer: [Yes] Justification: All external research assets used in this work, including existing mobile-agent frameworks, base models, and related benchmark or defense components, are publicly available or accessed under their respective licenses or API terms, and are properly cited in the paper. Answer: [Yes] Justification: The documentation can be found in the GitHub repository at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DIBench-5432. Answer: [N/A] Justification: The paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects. sections.heading: Appendix C Analyzing Determinants of In-Task Goal Deviation
sections.text: Results indicate that in-task goal deviation is not driven by a single variable; instead, it is jointly governed by six factor categories: (i) semantic coverage of the attack paradigm , (ii) agent-framework decision constraints , (iii) base-model characteristics , (iv) injection-carrier visibility and semantic weight , (v) interface structure across applications , and (vi) task type . We synthesize evidence from Tables 3 , 5 , 8 , and 9 , together with Figures 5 ,and 6 (injection carriers, cross-application, task types, and decision dynamics), and analyze each factor in detail. (1) Attack paradigm: stronger semantic coverage yields a higher ASR upper bound and better cross-environment stability. Attacks with “context overriding / instruction rewriting” semantics (i.e., Context Ignore and Combined ) achieve higher and more stable ASR than Naive and Escape . In Commerce (Table 3 ), Mobile-Agent-V3 + Qwen3-VL increases from 11.0%/12.9% under Naive/Escape to 44.6% under Context Ignore and 52.2% under Combined ; in Simulator (Table 5 ), it rises from 18.7%/19.3% to 43.3%/49.8%. Once an injection can override task context and provide an executable substitute instruction, it shifts probability mass toward the target candidate, raising ASR and improving cross-environment consistency. (2) Framework modulation: the same attack exhibits different tractability across frameworks, with model–framework interactions. Attack strength depends not only on the attack but also on framework-imposed constraints and action policies, and relative vulnerability varies with the base model. Under Qwen3-VL, Mobile-Agent-V3 and Mobile-Agent-E show high ASR under strong attacks in both environments: in Commerce (Table 3 ), Combined reaches 52.2%/50.3%, and in Simulator (Table 5 ), 49.8%/48.4%; in contrast, Mobile-Agent-V2 is lower (24.3%/27.9% for Context Ignore/Combined in Simulator ). Under Qwen2.5-VL, however, AppAgent attains 44.5% ASR under Combined in Simulator , surpassing Mobile-Agent-V3 (30.7%) and Mobile-Agent-V2 (25.6%). This suggests that “framework vulnerability” is not monotonic in the framework alone but emerges from interactions between framework decision constraints and base-model alignment characteristics. With frameworks and environments fixed, strong semantic-coverage attacks show a stable ASR hierarchy: general-purpose open-source models attain the highest ASR, specialized open-source models are lower, and closed-source models are generally lowest. With Mobile-Agent-V3 in Simulator (Table 8 ), Qwen3-VL achieves 43.3%/49.8% under Context Ignore/Combined , while Qwen2.5-VL reaches 31.8%/30.7%; GUI-Owl drops to 19.9%/19.3%, and closed-source models decrease further (e.g., DoubaoSeed-1.6 5.4%/7.5%, Gemini-3-Flash 5.0%/8.7%, GPT-5.2 5.9%/3.8%). Overall, general open-source models are more susceptible to instruction-style semantic overriding, while specialized open-source and closed-source models are more resistant, plausibly because general models emphasize broad instruction following and UI-semantic compliance, whereas specialized models rely more on structured grounding and closed-source models may incorporate stronger defenses and more conservative policies. (4) Injection carriers: gains are dominated by “readability × \times semantic weight”, with Title most effective but subject to saturation. Stable target steering occurs only when injections appear in high-weight semantic regions that the model can directly read; among carriers, Title coverage is typically most effective, while additional coverage may saturate or even degrade performance. In Table 9 , across frameworks and both base models, Title/Cover coverage usually yields ASR in the 20%–50% range and accounts for nearly all peak values, whereas Pert. is consistently lower (about 6%–16%) and never attains the maximum (“Summary # Max” = 0). Title+Cover also does not guarantee stronger attacks: under Qwen3-VL+Combined , the ASR of Mobile-Agent-E drops from 48.8% (Title) to 33.0%, Mobile-Agent-V3 from 49.9% to 40.6%, and AppAgent from 37.0% to 30.1%. This suggests Title carries high semantic weight, but multi-region coverage may be redundant and saturate attention; it may also reflect resolution/legibility effects or model–pipeline differences across regions. By contrast, Pert. behaves as weak noise: under the current implementation, UI rendering often disrupts target alignment, preventing perturbations from reliably encoding executable instructions and resulting in consistently low attack success; nevertheless, such rendering-layer anomalies can still cause agent decisions to deviate substantially from normal behavior. Frameworks and models mainly amplify or suppress these pre-existing vulnerabilities; while peak heights and secondary peak locations may shift, the overall pattern of which apps are more sensitive or robust is rarely overturned.
