(6) Task types: constraint strength determines “whether steering is possible”, while verifiability determines “whether steering leads to wrong selections”. Strong attacks exhibit a consistent stratification across task types: tighter constraints make tasks harder to steer, whereas tasks that rely on continuous attribute ranking with high UI verification cost are more vulnerable to “completion with targeted mis-selection”. Figure 6 shows that under attack, Open-ended tasks shift substantial probability mass to Correct(Target) , reflecting preference rewriting without necessarily increasing errors, and Exact Match tasks maintain high Correct rates under both no-attack and attack conditions with limited growth in Wrong(Target) . In contrast, Cost and Quality/Pop tasks show a pronounced increase in Wrong(Target) under Combined Attack, becoming the dominant error source, while Spatio-Temporal tasks exhibit mixed behavior with increases in both Wrong(Target) and Wrong(Non-Target) . Overall, discrete entity predicates impose strong constraints that limit steering outside A ⁡ ( I , C ) A(I,C) , whereas continuous ranking tasks become susceptible once injections reduce attribute comparison and verification while preserving task completion. Figure 6: Selection distribution by task type on Simulator under No Attack (N.) vs. Combined Attack (A.) across agent frameworks and model families, showing shifts among Correct(Target), Wrong(Target), and Wrong(Non-Target) (stacked). Takeaway. In-task goal deviation strength emerges from a multiplicative coupling of factors: strong semantic-coverage attacks raise the ASR upper bound, but stable steering depends on framework decision constraints, base-model alignment/defenses, whether injections enter high-weight readable regions (e.g., Title), and the structural limits imposed by the app interface and task. Thus, attacks are not uniformly strong across settings; they are jointly amplified or suppressed by the model–framework combination within what the decision pathway permits.

sections.heading: NeurIPS Paper Checklist
sections.text: 1. Claims Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The main claims in the abstract and introduction are aligned with the paper’s contributions. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper. • The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. A [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers. • The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings. • It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper. 2. Limitations Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Section 5 explicitly discusses limitations and future work. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper. • The authors are encouraged to create a separate “Limitations” section in their paper. • The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be. • The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated. • The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon. • The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size. • If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness. • While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations. 3. Theory assumptions and proofs Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and a complete (and correct) proof? Answer: [N/A] Justification: The paper does not present theoretical theorems or formal proof results. The mathematical content is limited to benchmark definitions and evaluation metrics in Section 3.3. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results. • All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and cross-referenced. • All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems. • The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short proof sketch to provide intuition. • Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material. • Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced. 4. Experimental result reproducibility Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Sections 3 and 4 describe the benchmark construction, paired evaluation protocol, metrics, repeated-run setting, agent frameworks, base models, and defense hooks. Appendix B further reports implementation details and compute infrastructure, and the paper provides an anonymized code repository. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • If the paper includes experiments, a [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not. • If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable. • Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed. • While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example (a) If the contribution is primarily a new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm. (b) If the contribution is primarily a new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully. (c) If the contribution is a new model (e.g., a large language model), then there should either be a way to access this model for reproducing the results or a way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset). (d) We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results. 5. Open access to data and code Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental material? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The abstract provides an anonymized code repository, and Section 3.2 states that normalized benchmark entries, annotations, injection specifications, labels, and metadata are packaged for release. The release is intended to support cross-framework reproduction and stratified analysis. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that paper does not include experiments requiring code. • Please see the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines ( https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy ) for more details. • While we encourage the release of code and data, we understand that this might not be possible, so [No] is an acceptable answer. Papers cannot be rejected simply for not including code, unless this is central to the contribution (e.g., for a new open-source benchmark). • The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to reproduce the results. See the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines ( https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy ) for more details. • The authors should provide instructions on data access and preparation, including how to access the raw data, preprocessed data, intermediate data, and generated data, etc. • The authors should provide scripts to reproduce all experimental results for the new proposed method and baselines. If only a subset of experiments are reproducible, they should state which ones are omitted from the script and why. • At submission time, to preserve anonymity, the authors should release anonymized versions (if applicable). • Providing as much information as possible in supplemental material (appended to the paper) is recommended, but including URLs to data and code is permitted. 6. Experimental setting/details Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The paper specifies the task suite, environments, injected-instance generation, paired benign/injected protocol, repeated evaluation with matched seeds, metrics, agent frameworks, base models, and defense settings in Sections 3 and 4. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • The experimental setting should be presented in the core of the paper to a level of detail that is necessary to appreciate the results and make sense of them. • The full details can be provided either with the code, in appendix, or as supplemental material. 7. Experiment statistical significance Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments? Answer: [No] Justification: The paper reports empirical averages from a large-scale paired benchmark evaluation. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper. • The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions). • The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to a library function, bootstrap, etc.) • The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors). • It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean. • It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report a 2-sigma error bar than state that they have a 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified. • For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates). • If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text. 8. Experiments compute resources Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the computer resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce the experiments? Answer: [No] Justification: Appendix B reports the local compute infrastructure used in our experiments. We do not report per-experiment runtime or total compute cost because the evaluation pipeline combines local execution, Android emulation, mobile UI interaction, and hosted closed-source model APIs; consequently, wall-clock time depends on factors such as API latency, provider-side scheduling, and UI interaction overhead that are not directly observable or consistently controlled by the authors. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • The paper should indicate the type of compute workers CPU or GPU, internal cluster, or cloud provider, including relevant memory and storage. • The paper should provide the amount of compute required for each of the individual experimental runs as well as estimate the total compute. • The paper should disclose whether the full research project required more compute than the experiments reported in the paper (e.g., preliminary or failed experiments that didn’t make it into the paper). 9. Code of ethics Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines ? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The paper includes an ethics statement explaining that real-app evaluations use fixed decision states and screenshot-level injections only, without publishing injected content, modifying third-party platforms, executing transactions, or collecting private user data. The benchmark is released for measurement and defense research rather than one-click attack deployment. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the authors have not reviewed the NeurIPS Code of Ethics. • If the authors answer [No] , they should explain the special circumstances that require a deviation from the Code of Ethics. • The authors should make sure to preserve anonymity (e.g., if there is a special consideration due to laws or regulations in their jurisdiction). 10. Broader impacts Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Sections 1, 5, and the ethics statement discuss the positive impact of improving decision-integrity evaluation for mobile GUI agents, as well as negative or dual-use risks from deceptive UI injections and potential misuse. The paper also explains safeguards used to avoid harm to users, merchants, and platforms during evaluation. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that there is no societal impact of the work performed. • If the authors answer [N/A] or [No] , they should explain why their work has no societal impact or why the paper does not address societal impact. • Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations. • The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied to particular applications, let alone deployments. However, if there is a direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that a generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster. • The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology. • If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how a system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML). 11. Safeguards Question: Does the paper describe safeguards that have been put in place for responsible release of data or models that have a high risk for misuse (e.g., pre-trained language models, image generators, or scraped datasets)? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The paper describes safeguards for the dual-use benchmark: commercial-app injections are performed only at the screenshot level, no content is published to live platforms, no transactions are executed, no private user data is collected, and the release is positioned for measurement and defense research with dataset documentation. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper poses no such risks. • Released models that have a high risk for misuse or dual-use should be released with necessary safeguards to allow for controlled use of the model, for example by requiring that users adhere to usage guidelines or restrictions to access the model or implementing safety filters. • Datasets that have been scraped from the Internet could pose safety risks. The authors should describe how they avoided releasing unsafe images. • We recognize that providing effective safeguards is challenging, and many papers do not require this, but we encourage authors to take this into account and make a best faith effort. 12. Licenses for existing assets Question: Are the creators or original owners of assets (e.g., code, data, models), used in the paper, properly credited and are the license and terms of use explicitly mentioned and properly respected? Answer: [Yes] Justification: All external research assets used in this work, including existing mobile-agent frameworks, base models, and related benchmark or defense components, are publicly available or accessed under their respective licenses or API terms, and are properly cited in the paper. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not use existing assets. • The authors should cite the original paper that produced the code package or dataset. • The authors should state which version of the asset is used and, if possible, include a URL. • The name of the license (e.g., CC-BY 4.0) should be included for each asset. • For scraped data from a particular source (e.g., website), the copyright and terms of service of that source should be provided. • If assets are released, the license, copyright information, and terms of use in the package should be provided. For popular datasets, paperswithcode.com/datasets has curated licenses for some datasets. Their licensing guide can help determine the license of a dataset. • For existing datasets that are re-packaged, both the original license and the license of the derived asset (if it has changed) should be provided. • If this information is not available online, the authors are encouraged to reach out to the asset’s creators. 13. New assets Question: Are new assets introduced in the paper well documented and is the documentation provided alongside the assets? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The documentation can be found in the GitHub repository at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DIBench-5432. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not release new assets. • Researchers should communicate the details of the dataset/code/model as part of their submissions via structured templates. This includes details about training, license, limitations, etc. • The paper should discuss whether and how consent was obtained from people whose asset is used. • At submission time, remember to anonymize your assets (if applicable). You can either create an anonymized URL or include an anonymized zip file. 14. Crowdsourcing and research with human subjects Question: For crowdsourcing experiments and research with human subjects, does the paper include the full text of instructions given to participants and screenshots, if applicable, as well as details about compensation (if any)? Answer: [N/A] Justification: The paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects. • Including this information in the supplemental material is fine, but if the main contribution of the paper involves human subjects, then as much detail as possible should be included in the main paper. • According to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics, workers involved in data collection, curation, or other labor should be paid at least the minimum wage in the country of the data collector. 15. Institutional review board (IRB) approvals or equivalent for research with human subjects Question: Does the paper describe potential risks incurred by study participants, whether such risks were disclosed to the subjects, and whether Institutional Review Board (IRB) approvals (or an equivalent approval/review based on the requirements of your country or institution) were obtained? Answer: [N/A] Justification: The paper does not report behavioral experiments with human subjects or user studies. The human involvement described in the manuscript is limited to benchmark annotation and verification, so IRB approval is not applicable unless required by the authors’ institution for annotation labor. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects. • Depending on the country in which research is conducted, IRB approval (or equivalent) may be required for any human subjects research. If you obtained IRB approval, you should clearly state this in the paper. • We recognize that the procedures for this may vary significantly between institutions and locations, and we expect authors to adhere to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics and the guidelines for their institution. • For initial submissions, do not include any information that would break anonymity (if applicable), such as the institution conducting the review. 16. Declaration of LLM usage Question: Does the paper describe the usage of LLMs if it is an important, original, or non-standard component of the core methods in this research? Note that if the LLM is used only for writing, editing, or formatting purposes and does not impact the core methodology, scientific rigor, or originality of the research, declaration is not required. Answer: [Yes] Justification: Section 3.2 describes the use of GPT-5.2 for initial candidate parsing and acceptable-set label proposal, followed by human verification and adjudication. Since this LLM usage affects benchmark construction rather than merely writing or formatting, it is appropriately disclosed. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the core method development in this research does not involve LLMs as any important, original, or non-standard components. • Please refer to our LLM policy in the NeurIPS handbook for what should or should not be described.

Learn more × Back to arXiv License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.06898v1 [cs.CR] 29 Sep 2026 DIBench: Benchmarking Decision Integrity of GUI-based Mobile Agents Under Deceptive Injections Li Hu Kanghua Mo Yingbin Jin Qingqing Ye Haibo Hu Affiliation: Department of Electrical and Electronic Engineering, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University Abstract As GUI-based mobile agents rapidly progress, rigorous safety evaluation of their autonomous decision-making in realistic app interfaces becomes increasingly critical. Existing benchmarks mainly focus on execution-level anomalies using task success or hijack rates, but fail to capture the in-task goal deviation risk in multi-candidate selection tasks, where the decision may be steered toward an attacker-specified target, even in violation of instruction-implied constraints (e.g., cheapest/highest-rated), without any overt execution anomalies. We present DIBench , a decision integrity benchmark for measuring this risk in mobile agents. DIBench covers 7 commercial and 3 simulated apps with 5 task types. Under a threat model restricted to non-privileged UI content, we construct 8 deceptive injection probe instantiations that can steer critical selections without overt anomalies. The benchmark includes 1,000 clean and 36,672 injected instances, with a unified protocol and integrity metrics for comparison. Experiments spanning 4 agent frameworks and 7 base models show that completion-based evaluation can overestimate agent trustworthiness and miss decision-integrity risks: deceptive injections steer selections and shift early action policies, inflating completion rates and creating a misleading illusion of safety. Common defenses, including detection, image preprocessing, and prompt reminders, yield inconsistent integrity gains. Overall, DIBench provides a unified, reproducible benchmark to quantify the risk of in-task goal deviation in mobile agents and enable comparable evaluations of safety defenses. 1 Introduction Recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have substantially improved cross-modal understanding and reasoning Bai et al. (2025a) ; OpenAI (2025) , enabling GUI mobile agents to autonomously perform multi-step interactions in real-world mobile apps Liu et al. (2025a) ; Rawles et al. (2024) ; Li et al. (2025) . Such agents are increasingly deployed in high-frequency scenarios—including shopping, food ordering, and travel planning—to filter options, verify details, and confirm choices Zhou et al. (2023) ; Lyu et al. (2025) . Because an agent’s output may directly trigger real transactions and shape security-sensitive decisions involving private or sensitive information, it is urgent to systematically characterize and validate the security and trustworthiness of mobile agent systems Chen et al. (2025b) ; Mathur et al. (2019) ; Lin et al. (2025) . Prior work has primarily evaluated mobile-agent security from the execution perspective Chen et al. (2025e) ; Chen et al. (2025c) ; Lee et al. (2026) ; Yang et al. (2025) ; Du et al. (2025) ; Liu et al. (2025b) , focusing on observable anomalies such as prompt-injection-induced task hijacking, unauthorized tool invocations, or interaction traces that visibly deviate from expected behavior. Accordingly, common metrics revolve around task completion rate and hijacking success rate Liu et al. (2025b) ; Liao et al. (2025) ; Lu et al. (2025) ; Evtimov et al. (2025) ; Chen et al. (2025a) , and many evaluations implicitly assume that flow-correct completion implies a trustworthy final choice Kara et al. (2025) ; Yehudai et al. (2025) . However, in real scenarios where multi-candidate selection is central, this assumption does not always hold Kang et al. (2025) ; Gebreegziabher et al. (2026) ; Xue et al. (2023) . In multi-candidate selection tasks on mobile devices, an agent may complete the workflow without privilege escalation, hijacking, or anomalous trajectories, yet still make a manipulated final selection Yang et al. (2024) ; Gebreegziabher et al. (2026) ; Kim et al. (2024) . We define this as In-Task Goal Deviation : under deceptive injection, the agent completes the task but its final choice is redirected toward an attacker-specified option, potentially even violating instruction-implied constraints (e.g., lowest price or highest rating) outside the acceptable set, thereby compromising decision integrity . Crucially, attackers need not alter the instruction or control flow: platform-permitted UI content (e.g., titles or images) can steer critical choices without overt anomalies, while completion-based signals are often insensitive—causing such deviations to be missed by evaluations focused on completion or trajectory anomalies. Although recent anecdotal evidence suggests that mobile agents can be steered by on-screen content during selection Yang et al. (2024) ; Wu et al. (2024) , the community still lacks a reproducible framework for measuring such decision-layer risks under controlled and comparable conditions. Key gaps remain: (1) no explicit security model for targeted in-task goal deviation; (2) the lack of a scalable benchmark suite of multi-candidate selection tasks spanning both commercial and simulated apps; and (3) no unified protocol or decision-integrity metrics for comparing agent frameworks, base models, and defenses. Our benchmark. To address this gap, we introduce DIBench , a benchmark for evaluating the decision integrity of mobile GUI agents in multi-candidate selection tasks. DIBench focuses on key decision states where the agent must compare candidates and select one according to instruction-implied constraints. For each task, we define an instruction I I , a candidate set C C , and an acceptable set A ⁡ ( I , C ) A(I,C) of semantically valid choices. We then construct paired benign and injected instances under matched task conditions, changing only UI-visible content at the critical decision point. This design allows DIBench to measure whether injected content causes targeted steering or decision degradation while controlling for the original task, candidate set, and non-visual context. DIBench covers both real-world and controlled environments. It includes 7 commercial mobile apps and 3 simulated apps across 5 categories of multi-candidate selection tasks, including exploratory, exact-match, cost-based, spatio-temporal, and quality/popularity-based decisions. To evaluate deceptive decision influence, we design 8 injection probe instantiations spanning textual overlays, image-embedded content, and visual perturbations. Overall, DIBench contains 1,000 benign instances and 36,672 injected instances, together with structured annotations for candidates, injection anchors, acceptable sets, target candidates, and paired evaluation. The benchmark further provides a unified configuration suite and standardized defense hooks, enabling comparable evaluation across agent frameworks, base models, and mitigation strategies under the same task and threat settings. Our findings. Using DIBench, we conduct evaluations spanning 4 mobile-agent frameworks and 7 base models across real commercial and simulated app settings. We make the following observations: (1) completion-oriented metrics can overestimate agent trustworthiness by missing decision-integrity risks, as deceptive injections can increase task completion while achieving high targeted steering rates (e.g., TCR rises from 42.0% to 72.4% with 45.8% ASR in commercial apps), creating a misleading illusion of improved safety under completion-based evaluation; (2) injections alter the decision process, reducing exploration and verification while inducing earlier commitment to injected targets; (3) common defenses remain unreliable, with detection recall dropping sharply on low-saliency injections and preprocessing sometimes increasing ASR; and (4) decision deviation is context-dependent, emerging from interactions among attack semantics, model behavior, framework constraints, UI structure, and task characteristics. Overall, DIBench provides a systematic testbed for evaluating decision-layer robustness of mobile GUI agents beyond execution-level safety metrics. 2 Background and Related Work Mobile GUI Agents and Multi-Candidate Decision Making. Mobile GUI agents typically operate in a closed observe–plan–act loop Tang et al. (2025a) ; Zhou et al. (2025) ; Gou et al. (2025) . Observations are derived from screenshots and accessibility trees, from which agents perform UI grounding and execute low-level actions such as tapping, scrolling, typing, and navigation Rawles et al. (2024) ; Hu et al. (2025) . Compared to scripted automation, MLLM-based agents can extract semantic cues from multimodal interfaces and conduct high-level planning across apps and pages, enabling complex workflows in real mobile environments Liu et al. (2025a) . In many real-world applications such as e-commerce and food delivery, task structure is inherently centered on comparison and selection over a candidate set Allouah et al. (2025) ; Wang et al. (2026) . Search results, filtered lists, and recommendation panels naturally form candidate sets, and agents must balance exploration (e.g., paging and filtering) with committing to a final choice. While existing evaluations often emphasize whether an agent completes the interaction flow, whether the within-set selection aligns with instruction semantics is a distinct and critical dimension of agent behavior. Decision-Layer Risks in Multi-Candidate Selection. A mobile agent can complete a task without any observable anomalies yet still make an attacker-steered choice at the selection stage Yang et al. (2024) ; Wu et al. (2024) ; Zhang et al. (2025) . In such cases, the agent performs browsing, filtering, and submission as expected, but ultimately selects a candidate promoted by deceptive UI content, potentially even violating the user’s objective. Because such risks involve no hijacking or execution anomalies, they are typically missed by existing execution-focused evaluations. However, these behaviors are often framed as isolated cases or capability gaps rather than as a systematic security risk Yang et al. (2024) . Consequently, decision-layer risks induced purely through platform-permitted UI content remain insufficiently formalized, and a reproducible, comparable evaluation framework is still missing. Figure 1: Overview of DIBench: Components, Construction Pipeline, and Extensible Paired Evaluation Suite. 3 DIBench Construction DIBench is designed to evaluate in-task goal deviation in multi-candidate selection tasks, where a mobile agent completes the workflow but its final choice is steered toward an attacker-specified target. To isolate this decision-layer risk, DIBench adopts a non-privileged UI-content threat model : the adversary can influence the agent only through platform-permitted on-screen content (e.g., titles or images), without modifying instructions, prompts, or control flow. Figure 1 illustrates DIBench. 3.1 Benchmark Components DIBench consists of three core components: environments, a task suite, and injection probes. Overall, it includes 7 commercial apps and 3 simulated apps across 5 task categories, with 1,000 benign instances and 36,672 injected instances, as summarized in Table 2 . 3.1.1 Environments To balance real-world validity and controllability, DIBench includes both real-world commercial applications and controlled simulated environments. Real-world commercial apps. We select 7 popular mobile apps—AliExpress, Amazon, Booking, Fantuan, Foodpanda, Tripadvisor, and Walmart—covering search, booking, and shopping scenarios. These apps provide realistic UI complexity and diversity. Due to ethical constraints, we do not upload adversarial images or injected merchant content to commercial platforms. Instead, we extract fixed decision states from real apps and apply controlled screenshot-level injections, keeping benign and injected inputs comparable while avoiding impacts on real users, merchants, or live services. Controlled simulated apps. For dynamic execution and mechanism analysis, we implement 3 controlled simulated apps: a Meituan-style food-ordering app, an online-shopping app, and a travel-itinerary planning app. These environments preserve multi-level browsing and multi-candidate selection patterns while reducing task-irrelevant UI noise, yielding deterministic and reproducible multi-step interactions with fixed candidate sets, hierarchy, and ordering. Crucially, they also support an end-to-end “ content publication/update → \rightarrow frontend rendering ” path, allowing injected content to be treated as a controlled variable for process-level analysis. 3.1.2 Task Suite Tasks are constructed for each app using unified templates, where the user objective and candidate set are explicitly specified to ensure a well-defined correct choice under benign conditions. Step 1: Benign instance construction and decision point localization. For each task, we execute a benign reference trajectory and identify the key decision point. We extract its evaluation input as a benign instance consisting of: (i) a screenshot of the critical selection interface and (ii) fixed non-visual context prior to selection (e.g., query history, filters, or sorting). The non-visual context is held constant across comparisons, yielding a reproducible decision state ⟨ screenshot , fixed context ⟩ \langle\textit{screenshot},\textit{fixed context}\rangle . Step 2: Structured candidate parsing and injection anchors. At each decision state, an MLLM-assisted annotation interface initializes candidate parsing C = { c 1 , … , c n } C=\{c_{1},\ldots,c_{n}\} by detecting candidate boundaries and extracting UI-visible text and attributes. These outputs serve only as preliminary drafts; human annotators verify, correct, and finalize all candidate sets, attributes, and anchors. Each candidate is assigned a stable ID, with injection anchors such as Title and Cover extracted. We release reusable annotations including (i) general annotations with candidate IDs and anchor identifiers for screenshot-level and backend injections, and (ii) screenshot-level annotations with pixel anchors and style parameters for controlled perturbations with minimal layout distortion. Step 3: Injection instance generation under a unified specification. Given benign instances and candidate anchors, injected instances are generated under a unified specification: decision state + target candidate + probe instantiation \textit{decision state}+\textit{target candidate}+\textit{probe instantiation} . For real commercial apps (screenshot-level injection), injected screenshots are produced via image-level overlay or embedding without modifying the underlying UI structure, reusing pixel anchors and style parameters from Step 2 to minimize non-semantic perturbations. For controlled simulated apps (backend injection), injections are applied to candidate fields (e.g., Title or Cover) along the content publication pipeline and rendered by the frontend during evaluation. Fixed candidate sets and UI structures ensure that injection semantics remain the primary controlled variable and enable process-level analysis. Table 3 and Appendix Table 5 show that deceptive injections can inflate , rather than reduce, task completion rate (TCR). Complete defense results are provided in Appendix. Detection-based defenses. Table 4 shows that detection achieves near-saturated recall on strong semantic-overwrite attacks (e.g., Context Ignore and Combined ). However, this advantage does not extend to more naturalistic injections: recall drops sharply to 18.2% and 21.2% for Naive and Escape , respectively, suggesting under-detection of low-saliency overlays. Moreover, adding planning signals does not consistently improve performance and can reduce recall below single-modality settings with substantial cross-framework variation. This pattern is consistent with the difficulty of extracting verifiable injection evidence from heterogeneous inputs, where additional modalities may introduce noise or conflicting signals. Image-processing-based defenses. Table 6 shows that preprocessing operations (e.g., noise, compression, and resizing) have inconsistent effects on ASR: the same method may reduce targeted steering in some cases but increase it in others. For example, noise injection can raise ASR from 45.8% to 60.0% in one setting while reducing it from 52.2% to 41.3% in another, with similar trends observed for compression and resizing. The root cause is that preprocessing is not semantic-aware: it can simultaneously weaken benign decision evidence and distort steering cues, sometimes reducing attribute verifiability and pushing agents toward locally salient signals that amplify selection shift. Prompt-based defenses. Table 7 shows that prompt-based defenses can substantially reduce ASR—often by over 30% for strong attacks—while sometimes improving COR. However, these gains are not consistent: in some configurations, prompts are ineffective or even increase ASR, and can incur noticeable COR drops. This suggests that prompt defenses act as soft constraints whose reliability depends on prompt orchestration and model compliance; reproducible decision-integrity gains likely require integrating key-attribute verification and UI-evidence referencing into the agent pipeline to reduce prompt sensitivity and avoid COR degradation. Takeaway. Existing defenses do not provide stable, generalizable improvements in decision integrity. Detection is sensitive to saliency and struggles with low-signal injections, preprocessing lacks semantic awareness and can distort decision evidence, and prompt-based defenses rely on fragile behavioral alignment. More fundamentally, these limitations stem from a mismatch: in-task goal deviation arises from failures in grounded evidence use and verification, whereas current general defenses do not enforce consistent, evidence-grounded decision-making. 4.4 Additional analysis We further examine factors that modulate the extent of in-task goal deviation; detailed results are provided in Appendix C . Deviation strength is not governed by a single factor, but by the joint effect of attack semantics, agent-framework constraints, base-model characteristics, injection-carrier visibility, app interface structure, and task type. Strong semantic-coverage probes raise the potential upper bound of target-specific steering, while the realized ASR is amplified or suppressed by the model–framework combination and by what the interface and task structure permit. These results suggest that in-task goal deviation is inherently context-dependent, and that robustness cannot be reliably inferred from a single attack setting or platform. Evaluating such risks therefore requires considering diverse decision contexts and the interactions among contributing factors. 5 Discussion and Future Work Decision integrity risks in mobile agents. Multimodal LLM-based mobile GUI agents can complete multi-step tasks in real applications, yet safety evaluation remains largely execution-centric (e.g., completion, absence of failures). Our results show that execution correctness and decision trustworthiness can be decoupled: agents may complete tasks without observable anomalies while being steered away from intended choices, resulting in in-task goal deviation . This risk arises from platform-permitted UI content (e.g., titles or images) that implicitly influences decisions without altering instructions or execution flow. Consequently, completion- and correctness-based metrics can underestimate decision-level risks and may even suggest improved performance under attack. This is critical in deployment, where users observe task completion but cannot detect subtle decision manipulation. Decision integrity should therefore be treated as a distinct layer in agent safety evaluation. Evaluating decision integrity. DIBench addresses this gap via paired (benign/injected) protocols and decision-integrity metrics, enabling cross-model comparison. TCR and COR fail to reflect manipulation and may create a false sense of safety, whereas ASR directly captures target steering. Trajectory analysis further shows that attacks weaken exploration and verification, inducing earlier commitment while preserving plausible interaction patterns. These findings highlight the need to evaluate evidence use and verification, beyond outcome-level metrics. Limitations and future work. DIBench is a reproducible academic benchmark for isolating decision-layer risks via controlled benign/injected comparisons. Our evaluation covers open research mobile-agent frameworks but not commercial or OEM-deployed assistants, such as AI phones or pre-installed voice assistants, limiting external validity. Still, DIBench captures a core risk: UI-visible content can influence model-driven selection without modifying user instructions or control flow. Future work should extend DIBench to production systems and long-horizon multi-decision tasks. Existing defenses are limited to general-purpose hooks, including detection, preprocessing, and prompt reminders; stronger evidence-grounded defenses, such as structured attribute comparison and pre-commit verification, remain important directions. Ethics statement. DIBench evaluates decision-level safety risks in mobile GUI agents under realistic UI conditions. A fully realistic setup would require publishing injected content to commercial platforms or interacting with live services, which could affect users, merchants, or platform operators without consent. We therefore avoid state-changing actions on external services: commercial-app evaluations use fixed decision states and screenshot-level injections only, without publishing content, modifying third-party platforms, executing transactions, or collecting private user data. Simulated apps are used for controlled mechanism analysis. We synthesize evidence from Tables 3 , 5 , 8 , and 9 , together with Figures 5 ,and 6 (injection carriers, cross-application, task types, and decision dynamics), and analyze each factor in detail. (1) Attack paradigm: stronger semantic coverage yields a higher ASR upper bound and better cross-environment stability. Attacks with “context overriding / instruction rewriting” semantics (i.e., Context Ignore and Combined ) achieve higher and more stable ASR than Naive and Escape . In Commerce (Table 3 ), Mobile-Agent-V3 + Qwen3-VL increases from 11.0%/12.9% under Naive/Escape to 44.6% under Context Ignore and 52.2% under Combined ; in Simulator (Table 5 ), it rises from 18.7%/19.3% to 43.3%/49.8%. Once an injection can override task context and provide an executable substitute instruction, it shifts probability mass toward the target candidate, raising ASR and improving cross-environment consistency. (2) Framework modulation: the same attack exhibits different tractability across frameworks, with model–framework interactions. Attack strength depends not only on the attack but also on framework-imposed constraints and action policies, and relative vulnerability varies with the base model. Under Qwen3-VL, Mobile-Agent-V3 and Mobile-Agent-E show high ASR under strong attacks in both environments: in Commerce (Table 3 ), Combined reaches 52.2%/50.3%, and in Simulator (Table 5 ), 49.8%/48.4%; in contrast, Mobile-Agent-V2 is lower (24.3%/27.9% for Context Ignore/Combined in Simulator ). Under Qwen2.5-VL, however, AppAgent attains 44.5% ASR under Combined in Simulator , surpassing Mobile-Agent-V3 (30.7%) and Mobile-Agent-V2 (25.6%). This suggests that “framework vulnerability” is not monotonic in the framework alone but emerges from interactions between framework decision constraints and base-model alignment characteristics. Overall, general open-source models are more susceptible to instruction-style semantic overriding, while specialized open-source and closed-source models are more resistant, plausibly because general models emphasize broad instruction following and UI-semantic compliance, whereas specialized models rely more on structured grounding and closed-source models may incorporate stronger defenses and more conservative policies. (4) Injection carriers: gains are dominated by “readability × \times semantic weight”, with Title most effective but subject to saturation. Stable target steering occurs only when injections appear in high-weight semantic regions that the model can directly read; among carriers, Title coverage is typically most effective, while additional coverage may saturate or even degrade performance. In Table 9 , across frameworks and both base models, Title/Cover coverage usually yields ASR in the 20%–50% range and accounts for nearly all peak values, whereas Pert. is consistently lower (about 6%–16%) and never attains the maximum (“Summary # Max” = 0). Title+Cover also does not guarantee stronger attacks: under Qwen3-VL+Combined , the ASR of Mobile-Agent-E drops from 48.8% (Title) to 33.0%, Mobile-Agent-V3 from 49.9% to 40.6%, and AppAgent from 37.0% to 30.1%. This suggests Title carries high semantic weight, but multi-region coverage may be redundant and saturate attention; it may also reflect resolution/legibility effects or model–pipeline differences across regions. By contrast, Pert. behaves as weak noise: under the current implementation, UI rendering often disrupts target alignment, preventing perturbations from reliably encoding executable instructions and resulting in consistently low attack success; nevertheless, such rendering-layer anomalies can still cause agent decisions to deviate substantially from normal behavior.
